Police manuals set out strict rules on their use, including in Victoria and Queensland, which warn tasers should only be deployed when there is a risk of serious physical injury.

But records on taser use are notoriously difficult to obtain. The data is collected by each state and territory police force and departments are not always forthcoming with it.

What we do have shows an increase in taser use in Australia's three most populous states.

In NSW, total taser incidents — which involve both pulling out a taser and discharging it — have more than doubled in the last three years after remaining steady since 2019.

Taser incidents have also more than doubled in Victoria in 2024, and Queensland's use has increased by a third in five years, although not all data is available in these states.

Taser reporting from the NSW and Victorian police forces also includes demographic information, which shows tasers are disproportionately used against Aboriginal people.

Emma Ryan, a criminologist at Deakin University who has spent her career studying tasers, believes "mission creep" is occurring.

"Mission creep is where a weapon is introduced for a particular purpose, but the mission creeps outside what it was intended to do in the first place," she said.

"So if a police officer pulled a firearm out in a lot of the cases that we see around tasers, we'd be living in the Wild West."

Emma Ryan has been studying tasers for more than 20 years. (Four Corners: Sissy Reyes)

Tasers were marketed by the manufacturer, Axon, as a way to stop deadly police shootings.

But data from the Australian Institute of Criminology shows firearm deaths in Australia have not decreased since their introduction more than 20 years ago.

"If tasers were used or confined to situations where firearms would be appropriate, I probably wouldn't have a problem," Dr Ryan said.

"Tasers simply put the emphasis on coercion so much that it degrades good quality policing."

Are tasers used to 'protect life'?

Tasers are carried by police officers in every state and territory in Australia.

Right now, Queensland Police is spending $47 million on more than 6,500 new devices.

Victoria Police has rolled out 10,000 new devices and NSW Police recently updated its weapons.

NSW Police superintendent Pat Sharkey defended the force's rising use of tasers and cautioned against looking at "bulk statistical data".

"[Tasers are] a tactical option … often it is a situation that police are confronted by angry, argumentative people, maybe violence, and they do it to protect life, essentially," he said.

"I think for any criticism to be levelled, it needs to be done on the basis of the circumstances that exist in an individual situation."

NSW Police have been using the newer Taser 7 model since 2023. (Four Corners: Sissy Reyes)

Four Corners' analysis of coronial inquest findings and media reports since 2002 found 18 cases where a person died after being tasered by police.

In many of these instances a coroner found the taser was a contributing factor to the death or did not reach a conclusion on the cause.

In the last five years six people have died after they were tasered, including 95-year-old Clare Nowland in 2023.

The great-grandmother fell and suffered an inoperable brain bleed after being tasered at an aged care home by NSW police officer Kristian White. He was sacked and found guilty of manslaughter but avoided jail time.

Many of these recent cases have not been finalised by a coroner, including Ms Nowland's death.

NSW Police said it would be inappropriate to comment ahead of the inquest.

'Didn't actually have a right to use force'

Two years on, Stephen still struggles with how police treated him on his family farm.

His lawyer Jeremy King, who specialises in police misconduct cases, believes it could have ended very differently for Stephen if it were not for the dash cam footage.

"He was tasered multiple times. He was pepper sprayed. Force was used against him on his own family property. The fact that no charges were laid against him is extremely telling," Mr King said.

"He wasn't posing any threat and so therefore, under their own rules and under their own manual, they didn't actually have a right to use force against him.

"This whole incident raises questions to me about whether any of the officers were appropriately trained."

Stephen sued Victoria Police for unlawful arrest and battery. The case recently settled with police paying Stephen $250,000 in compensation plus his legal costs.

A complaint about the incident has also been made to Victoria's Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission.

IBAC declined to comment on whether it was looking at the complaint, but Victoria Police confirmed to Four Corners that the agency has investigated.

Stephen was not charged over the incident and received a compensation payout. (Four Corners: Sissy Reyes)

'She was so vulnerable'

In Queensland, Tiejwana's family and her legal team have been fighting for six years for police to be held accountable for what they did to her.

Lawyer Peter O'Brien is still bewildered by the decision to use a taser against a vulnerable child who police were trying to interview about allegations of sexual abuse against her.

"Police have a difficult job to do and this was obviously a pretty fluid and dynamic situation, but … the use of force was plainly excessive and unlawful," he said.

"It was striking for the reason that she was so vulnerable.

"Tasers should not be used against children at all, in my view."

Robyn wanted the officers involved to lose their jobs but an internal investigation cleared them of any misconduct.

Robyn wants police held to account for tasering her daughter. (Four Corners: Sissy Reyes)

Tiejwana's family has sued Queensland Police, claiming the tasering, use of force and her arrest was cruel, degrading and unlawful treatment.

Mr O'Brien, who specialises in these types of cases against police, said he had often seen tasers used unnecessarily and inappropriately.

"This is not a one-off," he said.

Queensland Police told Four Corners that "it would not be appropriate" to comment on the incident while it was the subject of legal proceedings.

It also defended its use of tasers by officers and said the devices were part of "a range of tactical options".

"[They] are used in accordance with strict policy, and their use must be justified, necessary and proportionate in the circumstances," a spokesperson said.

Life for Tiejwana is different now. Since she was tasered, she cannot go to the toilet and has to wear pull-ups. Her seizures have also worsened and happen more often.

"They [police] can't do that to people and think they can get away with it," Robyn said.

"Her life is hard enough without that happening to her."

Watch Four Corners' full investigation, Taser Tactics, on Monday May 4 from 8:30pm on ABC TV and ABC iview.

World.title: Trump and populist politics dominant Albanese's first year of second term
World.content:
Anthony Albanese says the United States is "playing a different role" in the world under President Donald Trump, forcing Australia and allies to adjust how they respond to unexpected conflicts.

In a wide-ranging interview reflecting on the first year of his second term, the prime minister told ABC Radio National Saturday Extra that Mr Trump's "America first" mandate, which has included imposing punishing tariffs on allies and not giving them a heads-up before launching war in Iran, has seen Australia band together more closely with other middle powers.

"The United States is playing a different role now," he said.

"It has retreated from some of its previous positions on economic policy, for example, when it comes to protectionism and the imposition of tariffs [and] that's a very different position from the historic pro-market position that the United States has held.

" The fact that it made the decision, without consulting allies, to launch the war on Iran, is a different position from where they've been historically and the world is adjusting to that change. "

He told Saturday Extra that while the US remained Australia's "most important ally", it "doesn't mean that we're not out there engaging with others".

It echoed comments he made last week that Australia was not in a "monogamous relationship" with the United States and was instead "out there dating in our region".

He pointed to cooperation between Australia and countries across Europe and Asia, as well as Canada.

Middle powers must work together

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney made a splash with a speech in January, declaring the post-war international order was over and urging smaller countries to band together "because if you are not at the table, you are on the menu".

Mr Albanese was asked if America's northern neighbour was freer to critique the US than Australia because of the AUKUS partnership.

But he pushed back by saying Mr Carney actually took elements from his speech to the United Nations in New York last year.

"Mark Carney used some of the exact language that I used," he said.

"He took from that speech the view very strongly that I put: that middle powers needed to work together."

King speaks to Congress In a speech that was supposed to be apolitical, King Charles hits on some hot-button issues that are fuelling controversies around the Trump administration.

Mr Albanese also delivered a glowing review of King Charles's speech to the US Congress this week, which has been noted for its reflection on NATO, defending Ukraine and climate protection.

"It was terrific," Mr Albanese said, focusing on how Australia and the UK could continue to have deep relationships with the US while maintaining differences.

"I have a constructive relationship with President Trump, as people have seen, and that's important as Australia's prime minister, but … that doesn't mean that we're synonymous."

One Nation part of right-wing populist 'phenomenon'

Community division has marred much of Mr Albanese's second term, from tensions over the Middle East and the rising interest in populist politics, to pushback against Welcome to Country ceremonies.

Mr Albanese pointed to a trend of political movements romanticising the past and of people drifting to the far edges of political discourse, often led by social media, as a cause of social division.

"One of the factors I think that leads to a polarisation across the world [are] people going into corridors and they just dig deeper and go further to the far left or far right, because that's where the algorithms lead them," he said.

While some people, he noted, were left feeling exposed by the pace of change, he also highlighted the importance of progress.

He said the trajectory of change was rarely straight, pointing to his support of the Voice to Parliament, at odds with his party's racist origins.

"One of its planks was the White Australia policy. We only had four," he said of Labor a century ago.

"History has moved forward and history will continue to move forward, but it doesn't move forward in a straight line."

Asked about the failure of the Voice to Parliament referendum, Mr Albanese conceded it had spurred some people to share divisive views.

"It was unfortunate, but we respected the outcome and at the same time, I think it did lift up the debate about Indigenous issues, and we need to have that," he said.

Mr Albanese said he found it "disconcerting" some Anzac Day dawn services had been marred by the booing during Welcome to Country remarks.

While the booing has broadly been condemned as "un-Australian" and disrespectful, it has sparked a conversation, led largely by members of the opposition, about whether Welcomes to Country were being overused.

He said the ceremonies were important acts of politeness.

"For them to be booed, is, in my view, a break with the Australian spirit."

The Prime Minister signalled he wants to focus on uniting the nation, as he embarks on the remainder of his second term as leader.

World.title: What we know about the ISIS-linked Australian families in Syria
World.content:
Four Australian women, their children and grandchildren are stuck in limbo in Syria after leaving a refugee camp housing family members of suspected Islamic State fighters.

Last week the group left the Al Roj camp in north-east Syria with the goal of heading to the capital, Damascus, and flying home to Australia.

But after Syrian authorities said they prevented the group from reaching the airport because of strong rhetoric from the Australian government, it is unclear what their next moves will be.

The ABC can reveal the group includes three generations of the same family.

Here is what we know about them.

Kawsar Abbas

Kawsar Abbas, 54, is from Melbourne.

She is the wife of Mohammed Ahmad, who ran a charity to support the people of Syria.

Mohammed Ahmad spoke to the ABC from detention in Syria in 2019. (ABC News)

The Australian Federal Police suspected the charity of funnelling cash to Islamic State.

In 2019, Mohammed Ahmad told the ABC that he and his family got trapped in Syria after travelling from the charity's headquarters in Turkey to attend the wedding of his son, Omar, in 2014.

Mohammed said soon after arriving in Syria, he realised Omar had sworn allegiance to Islamic State. Omar also kept a Yazidi slave, who Ahmad said was treated well.

Mohammed insisted he was never an Islamic State supporter, but said he was imprisoned in north-east Syria when IS was defeated.

From 2019: How this Australian aid worker's family were detained in Syria An ABC investigation reveals how one Australian aid worker and 11 of his family members ended up dead or being detained in Syria. Mohammed Ahmad says he does not pose a threat but his chances of returning to his home country appear slim.

"The Australian government … have nothing to worry about from my side," he told the ABC back in 2019.

"Australia is really my home country. I've been living there since I was a little kid.

"I would rather be judged in Australia than here."

In 2019, ahead of the Syrian winter, Kawsar Abbas told the Sydney Morning Herald she was worried about the health of the children in the camp.

"One of our tents flooded and then it dried up … but winter is not going to be like that. It's not going to dry up," she said.

Zahra Ahmed

Zahra married notorious Islamic State recruiter Muhammad Zahab, who died in an air strike. (Four Corners)

Zahra, 33, is the eldest daughter of Mohammed and Kawsar Abbas.

She is the widow of notorious Islamic State recruiter Muhammad Zahab, who died in an air strike in 2018.

In 2024 Zahra told an SBS documentary that the women had no choice but to follow when some male members of her family joined ISIS.

"I didn't make this bed," she told SBS.

"We are now forced to suffer for the decisions that other people — other male influencers — made on our behalf, and now they are all gone and we are left to suffer with our kids."

From 2019: Infiltrating Australia's jihadi recruiting network Tracing their journeys from quiet Australian suburbia to IS brides, Four Corners exposes the secret network that led many women to Islamic State.

In 2019 Zahra and her family told the Sydney Morning Herald they had been doing humanitarian work in Syria when the Islamic State's so-called caliphate closed its borders, preventing them from leaving.

"We're willing to talk [to the Australian government], and we're willing to … share our stories," Zahra told the newspaper.

"But they haven't even tried to come and reach out to us, and when we ask they don't want to."

In 2019, Four Corners reported that Muhammad Zahab, who was a maths teacher in Sydney, had recruited many of his friends and family to join him in Islamic State-occupied Syria.

He married Zahra, his second wife, in Syria.

Zeinab Ahmed

Zeinab Ahmed told the ABC the camps in Syria were not safe for children. (ABC News: Haybar Othman)

Zeinab, 31, is the second-eldest daughter of Mohammed and Kawsar Abbas.

She last spoke to the ABC from the Al Roj camp in 2025 and made an impassioned plea to the Australian government to help get the group home, saying she feared for her safety and the lives of her children.

"It's not a place for a child to be, and every day, especially for the past two months … it's just getting harder," Zeinab told the ABC.

"There's a street [in the camp] — it's called Australia Street. We live closely, we have a strong connection because we all have the same motive. We all want to get home."

From 2025: Australian women who lived under ISIS want to come home Australian women who lived in the terror group's so-called caliphate speak from detention camps in Syria, begging the federal government to bring them home.

At the time she revealed that Australian officials had travelled to the camp to meet with the women and children in 2022.

The officials interviewed families and carried out identity checks and DNA tests.

One of the architects of the operation to get the families out of Al Roj, Sydney GP Jamal Rifi, had paid for the passports and carried them to Syria.

Months later four families were repatriated to Australia.

"They took the first group and we were so happy that some of us were getting out, some of our kids will be saved," Zeinab said at the time.

Janai Safar

Janai was studying health science in Australia before she left in 2015 to travel to Islamic State-occupied Syria.

The 32-year-old had a child in Syria in 2016.

She was married to an Islamic State fighter who died in 2017, the ABC has been told.

Janai was among the women whom Four Corners met in the Al-Hol camp in 2019.

Loading...

Back in 2019, Janai told the Australian newspaper that she got married after arriving in Syria, then stayed at home and looked after her child.

She said while she did not regret travelling to Syria, she feared being treated like a criminal if she ever returned to Australia.

"I didn't train or kill anyone," the masthead quoted her as saying.

"I just sat at home, and they will put me in jail, they will take my child off me. Why? I'm a Muslim."

Her father told the newspaper she was a "stubborn but kind-hearted" woman who posed no threat to Australia.

Her grandfather John Crockett told the ABC in 2019 it would be better for the families to return to Australia than to languish in camps in Syria.

"If some of them are going to go to jail when they come home it's far better for them to be in prison back here and do a term of whatever they've been convicted of," he said.

"At least if they come back here and they're jailed, we'll be able to go and see them."

A murky future

Accompanying the four women are nine children, who the ABC is not naming.

The ABC understands 21 Australian women and children still remain inside the Al Roj camp.

In February, the ABC revealed the identities of all 11 Australian women in the camp after seeing a handwritten list of their names.

Many of the women had previously spoken to the ABC, including as far back as 2019, when Four Corners gained access to north-eastern Syria.

Most of the women have been stuck in Syrian refugee camps since the collapse of Islamic State in 2019.

Some of their children were born in camps such as Al Roj.

Many of the women have claimed that they were not supporters of Islamic State but victims, and were lured into travelling to Syria under false pretences.

Some legal and human rights groups have also warned that the group, particularly the children, face a grave risk of further radicalisation if left to languish in the camps.

The ABC has made repeated attempts to contact the group, their family, and their supporters.

World.title: How a 'loner' went from a life of privilege to Bondi gunman
World.content:
A brother-in-law of Sajid Akram says the Bondi gunman spent years trying to isolate and control his wife and children, including eldest son Naveed. ( )

Even to members of his own family, Sajid Akram was an unusually secretive man.

To this day, his Australian brother-in-law, Michael, says he does not know how Akram met his sister Venera before they married. Michael, who asked not to be identified by his real name, says he never knew Akram to have his own mobile phone, which he found strange.

"He was so hard to have a conversation with," Michael says.

Akram revealed little about his work life, and almost nothing about his friends or his interests, he says.

A chilling exception, according to Michael, was an announcement Akram once made out of the blue. He says it was more than a decade before Akram and his son, Naveed Akram, used legally obtained weapons in an anti-Semitic massacre at Bondi last December.

"[Sajid] said, 'I want to get a gun licence, brother,'" he says.

"I said, 'What do you want a gun for?'

"He said, 'I want to go hunting.'

"I said, 'You're not a hunter.'"

It's unclear if hunting ever was a real interest for Akram.

But years later, he would rely on the same explanation to cover his tracks while planning Australia's worst ever terror attack.

In the year leading up to the Bondi attack, Akram took his son on a series of trips west of Sydney to a rural property. It's owned by a Greek army veteran who asked to be identified only as "Jimmy". Jimmy wanted the pair to hunt the foxes that menaced his baby goats and lambs, but instead they practised shooting at cardboard targets.

"I … asked him, 'Why you shoot so many times and you scare away my animal[s]?'" Jimmy says.

He says the only animals Sajid Akram showed interest in shooting were the unwanted farm dogs Jimmy had earmarked for the RSPCA.

"The father [told] me, "[If] you want, I'll kill them right now."

Sajid and Naveed Akram went shooting but showed no interest in hunting, a farm owner says. ( )

Jimmy declined.

That was his only conversation with Akram, Jimmy says. The son did all the talking — not that Jimmy knew they were related, since Naveed Akram had said they were "friends".

Jimmy says when the pair cut short their final stay at the farm last October, the son said he had to return to Sydney to care for a sick grandfather. In reality, Naveed Akram's grandfather had been dead for 16 years.

The Akrams' ability to deceive those around them — keeping secrets from family and intelligence services alike — set them apart from other extremists they had encountered in western Sydney. It enabled them to become one of the only father-son duos in the English-speaking world to carry out a terrorist attack.

Through the secrecy, Background Briefing has uncovered new details about their lives by searching public records and speaking to people who knew the family in Australia and overseas.

Andrew Aboud, one of Australia's leading forensic psychiatrists, says these findings help explain why the pair developed extremist views and crossed the threshold to violence.

Dr Aboud has worked with government, courts and police to help them understand the mind states of criminals — including the Wieambilla police killers for an inquest last year.

Psychiatrist Andrew Aboud says a father with "narcissistic" qualities sees his children as an extension of himself. ( )

He agreed, in a private capacity, to examine the results of Background Briefing's investigation into the Akrams and share his observations.

"When they share in a behaviour like this, one cannot ignore the relationship between them," he says.

" What type of a father was Sajid to Naveed? And how did Naveed respond to that? Was he vulnerable to being influenced adversely, or is it possible that it was the other way around? "

An 'upper-middle-class' background

Sajid Akram spent most of his life in Sydney’s outer western suburbs, but he was born and raised in relative privilege in India.

The family lived in a large ancestral home near a mosque in the old part of Hyderabad, and neighbours say his father served in the military.

Indian journalist Tawqeer Hussain, who worked with Background Briefing on this investigation, travelled to Hyderabad and spoke to former neighbours.

Hussain says Akram grew up in an "upper-middle-class" family ensconced in an aspirational, non-fundamentalist Muslim community.

"They are mostly into those IT sectors, very well educated, they're mostly into their jobs," he says. "They want to excel."

Sajid Akram grew up in an upper-middle class family, living in this house in Hyderabad's Old City. ( )

A former neighbour says Akram was "very straightforward — he didn't talk too much", while a family friend says he was "a jolly person [who] used to play cricket with us".

Akram seemed destined for a comfortable life.

He graduated with a commerce degree from a mid-range Indian university in 1996. The university president says records reveal Akram's marks were average.

His brother Shahed, by contrast, seems to have excelled.

By the end of the following year, Shahed Akram had graduated from medicine at a top university and was working as a doctor.

The family eventually moved into an expensive new house in a more prosperous neighbourhood closer to the city centre.

Sajid Akram's family in India moved to an expensive new house (right) in Hyderabad's inner-west after he migrated to Australia. ( )

But Sajid Akram didn't get to climb the ladder with them. He had already left the country for Australia.

Shahed Akram refused interview requests.

A secret wedding

Soon after arriving in Australia on a student visa in November 1998, Akram met the woman who was pivotal to his future.

Venera was the daughter of Italian migrants who grew up in Strathfield, in Sydney's Inner West.

Former neighbours Lorraine and Gary Grohmann say Venera's family was tight-knit and deeply Catholic. They remember congratulating Venera's parents on the day of her confirmation, when she wore a white lace dress.

Hear the full story Listen: inside the lives drawn together on the day of the Bondi tragedy. A three-part podcast by Background Briefing.

"They were very proud of the fact that their children were going through these different ceremonies within the church," Lorraine says.

"I always remember [Venera] laughing and giggling and being quite cute, but she was a soft girl. She didn't have much confidence."

Their marriage gave Akram a pathway to permanent residency in Australia but caused tension on both sides of the family.

Venera's brother Michael says the couple eloped, marrying in secret in a civil ceremony in Sydney, which was hurtful to her father in particular.

Hussain says in India, "some of the neighbours and some of the police officers confirmed to me that there was a resentment in the family about [Akram] being married to a Christian woman".

Dr Aboud says Akram's decision to marry a Christian woman suggests he did not arrive in Australia with a fundamentalist Islamic mindset.

"It sounds to me if he did develop any extreme, radicalised belief system, that happened later," he says.

While on the surface Akram was blending into Australian society, there were signs his new life was not working out as he might have hoped.

Michael says when he first met Akram, "he told me he worked in computers — but in all the time I knew him he never did". Instead, the commerce graduate ended up in relatively low-paying retail jobs. Michael says Akram "must have worked in every fruit shop in western Sydney", moving from job to job.

The same year Akram's family in India moved into their palatial new home in Hyderabad, he and Venera bought their first home — a duplex on a highway in Cabramatta. There, the couple began raising their three children, including their eldest, Naveed Akram.

Lorraine Grohmann says another of Venera's old neighbours, who was working in Cabramatta at the time, heard that she was "very under the thumb" of her husband.

'Lies and manipulation'

It gels with Michael's account of controlling behaviour by his brother-in-law towards Venera and their children. He says Akram himself was "a loner who was withdrawn". But he also isolated his wife and children from the extended family and discouraged the kids from forming outside friendships, Michael says.

Akram so often refused to join Venera at family events that people began joking his sister was "a widow", he says.

Police investigators at the scene of a raid on a Bonnyrigg home linked to the Bondi Beach shooters, on December 15 last year. ( )

Michael says he glimpsed the level of control Akram exercised over his sister one day when visiting the couple's second home in Bonnyrigg in outer western Sydney.

Michael says it was a family day and he brought several longnecks of beer to drink. He says despite Akram not being there, Venera said her husband would be furious about the beer and was "petrified" he would find out. Michael put the bottles in the bin. But he says Venera was so worried about Akram finding out, he had to take all the bottles with him when he left.

Michael says with Akram, there was "a lot of lies and manipulation".

"I never liked him," he says.

A relative says Sajid Akram isolated his children, including Naveed Akram, and discouraged them from friendships. ( )

This picture of Akram is less than complete, but Dr Aboud says it could be a window into how he raised his son Naveed Akram.

"One always must wonder about what it is that we don't know — but there's arrows pointing in the direction of Sajid having what we would call narcissistic qualities," Dr Aboud says.

" That type of individual is at the heart of it, an insecure person who is looking to control what's going on around him, whether it's controlling his partner, controlling his children. "

As a teenager, Naveed Akram seemed in some ways to be on a more promising trajectory than his father. After high school, he entered the workforce as an apprentice bricklayer, impressing co-workers with his attitude.

A veteran labourer, who asked to be identified only as William, says Naveed Akram "came across so innocent".

William says Naveed Akram was "exposed to the trade, and the Australian way of life [and] he wanted to be part of the team, he wanted to have a go".

The young man qualified as a bricklayer and could have gone on to become a builder earning serious money, William says.

"He made the grade … he had the world at his feet."

But Naveed Akram was straddling two worlds: on one side, his mother's extended family, and on the other, his seemingly alienated father. At some point, he tipped over into the latter.

'Sees son as extension of himself'

Sajid Akram did not seem a particularly observant Muslim when he arrived in Australia. But by 2019, he was taking his son to a mosque near their old home in Cabramatta. There, Akram introduced his son to a recruiter for a street preaching group.

That year, Naveed Akram appeared in an online video for the group, speaking to students about Islam. Six years out from Bondi, the video betrays none of "more extremist views if that was what he was holding", Dr Aboud says.

But soon, he was mingling with Islamic State sympathisers.

The president of the Cabramatta mosque says both Naveed Akram and his father attended a Ramadan retreat in June 2019. Here, the younger man spent time with a group of strangers that included at least one IS supporter, who was later convicted of terrorism offences. The group became confrontational and was asked to leave. That was the last time the Akrams were seen at the mosque, the president says.

Naveed Akram was investigated by ASIO over links to Islamic State supporters. ( )

Naveed Akram's association with IS supporters, who were arrested a month later, put him on the radar of the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (ASIO). ASIO investigated him for six months and in 2020 found there was no evidence he supported IS or was planning, considering or promoting any act of violence at the time. Investigators also interviewed Sajid Akram and found no evidence he was radicalised.

The finding is at odds with the account of a former undercover operative for ASIO known as Marcus.

He has told the ABC that Akram, who was furious that ASIO was investigating his son, expressed support for IS in a conversation with Marcus. Marcus claims Akram said that if Muslims could not do something for IS in Australia, they should travel abroad to join them. Marcus says he reported this to ASIO.

ASIO has dismissed Marcus's account, saying he is "unreliable and disgruntled" — which Marcus denies.

Dr Aboud says if Akram played an active role in radicalising his son, that would fit his apparent patterns of behaviour.

"An isolated man prone to secrecy, controlling, narcissistic, goes down a path where he is increasingly vulnerable, finds the cause, locks it in," Dr Aboud says.

" If the father has narcissistic qualities, then he has an entitled sense of ownership over his son. He sees his son as an extension of himself, and he doesn't have a problem in taking his son on that same journey. "

Two months after ASIO ended its investigation, Akram applied for a gun licence. He and his son joined a local gun club in Bonnyrigg. After a three-year wait, Akram received his licence, which gave him access to weapons the pair could use unsupervised.

While father and son bonded over guns, they appeared to detach from the rest of the family.

Michael says at Venera's 50th birthday party, in the year before the Bondi attack, Naveed Akram appeared noticeably distant and vaguely hostile.

"He just looked different. There was a darkness in his eyes," Michael says.

Akram had transferred his share of the family home to Venera. The marriage reportedly ended.

Dr Aboud says a marriage break-up has the potential to "fracture" a person like Akram.

"In a person who has narcissistic qualities, it will cause an injury deep inside his psychological framework. It could in fact destabilise him," he says.

Amid this downward spiral last October, the same month of their last shooting trip to Jimmy's remote farm, Akram and his son recorded the video that police allege explains their motives for the Bondi attack.

Police allege the video showed them in front of an IS flag with rifles against a wall, "condemning the acts of 'Zionists'". Its discovery on Naveed Akram's phone after the attack represents one of the few electronic footprints they left for law enforcement.

Their trip to the southern Philippines weeks before the attack raised suspicions of contact with other Islamist extremists. But so far, authorities have said there's no evidence of that — only of the Akrams spending most of their time together in a small, cheap hotel room in Mindanao.

The Philippines Army Bomb Squad seen searching the GV Hotel, where the two Bondi gunmen are believed to have stayed in November last year. ( )

While the Akrams were in the Philippines, the first public social media posts appeared promoting the Chanukah by the Sea festival in Bondi. Within three days, the Akrams were on a plane back to Australia.

Dr Aboud says the Akrams' ability to keep their plans and their views secret from those around them before the attack was highly unusual.

"That might have been underpinned by Sajid's natural tendency towards being very suspicious and not trusting people, and encouraging his son to do likewise," he says.

On December 14, father and son began firing on the Jewish festival crowd from a concrete bridge.

Suddenly, Akram left his son on the bridge to get closer to the crowd.

Out in the open, Akram was tackled and disarmed by a bystander.

Sajid Akram (right) was disarmed during the Bondi attack by Ahmed Al Ahmed. ( )

His son covered him with gunfire and called him back to the bridge.

" It took them both," Dr Aboud says."They were able to keep something a secret for a long period of time, and they were able to then enact it on the day. "

Credits

Reporter: Josh Robertson

Graphics: Sharon Gordon

Fact check: Justine Landis-Hanley

Supervising Producer: Max Chalmers

World.title: What is a town camp and what is life like there for Aboriginal people?
World.content:
The death of five-year-old Kumanjayi Little Baby in the Northern Territory has left a community in mourning and a nation heartbroken.

The little girl had been visiting family with her mother in what is known as a town camp when she was allegedly abducted, sparking a five-day search.

Jefferson Lewis, 47, has been arrested and is expected to be charged with her murder.

There are now calls from Senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price for an inquiry into this tragic death and the conditions of town camps.

But what exactly is a town camp and who lives in them?

Constantly changing population

Around the outskirts of Alice Springs, there are sixteen communities known as town camps, populated by Aboriginal families.

Riot erupts after Kumanjayi Little Baby's alleged killer arrested Wild scenes erupted on the streets of Alice Springs after the arrest of Jefferson Lewis over the alleged murder of five-year-old Kumanjayi Little Baby.

According to the last census, 1,055 people live permanently in the camps, in 256 households, with a median income of $757 per week.

But the population is constantly changing, as families, connected through kinship or culture, visit from the more remote parts of Australia, often to access health and other essential services.

The Old Timers, also known as Ilyperenye town camp, is where Kumanjayi Little Baby was allegedly abducted from, about 6 kilometres to the south of Alice Springs.

Tangentyere Council Aboriginal Corporation manages the town camps around Alice Springs, providing their social and infrastructure services.

Walter Shaw is a fourth-generation town camp resident. (ABC News: Matt Garrick )

The council's chief executive, Walter Shaw, explained they were set up in four points around Alice Springs — north, south, east and west — reflecting the "mindset of the old people".

"The proportion of people residing to the north of Alice Springs are very closely connected to northern remote communities. The town camps situated to the south … predominantly have a close connection and relationship to the southern communities," he said.

The town camps are organised to provide homes for distinct families and language groups. For example, at Inarlenge Little Sisters, the residents are Arrernte, Warlpiri, Luritja, Pitjantjatjara speakers.

Properties at the Hidden Valley town camp. (ABC Alice Springs: Samantha Jonscher )

The Old Timers camp is small, with nine houses.

"There's a mixture of language groups there, including the Warlpiri Aboriginal group, plus some southern speaking Aboriginal tribes," Mr Shaw said.

Why are camps located outside city or town centres?

Town camps were created out of necessity because of discriminatory policies and attitudes that prevented Aboriginal people from entering Alice Springs.

Many were denied the same rights as other territorians, to freely move about, work and participate in social activities.

Kumanjayi Little Baby went missing from a home in the Old Timers/Ilyperenye Aboriginal town camp on the outskirts of Alice Springs. (ABC News: Jessica Henderson)

Mr Shaw, a fourth-generation town camp resident, said the camps were officially recognised in the 70s because Aboriginal people were not provided with necessary government services, such as secure houses, running water, sewerage and garbage removal.

"So, the old people fought to secure land tenure arrangements throughout Alice Springs, and that's the inception of the town camps," he said.

"Later down the track, they established Tangentyere Council to provide services that were inadequately provided by the government in those days."

Children play in the midday sun at the Hidden Valley town camp near Alice Springs. (AAP: Dan Peled)

Today, the Northern Territory government is responsible for funding the camps' infrastructure and housing.

According to Aboriginal Housing NT, their locations can hold special, historical significance, as a "traditional ceremonial camping area".

Town camps were, in some cases, established for short stays, but over time have become more permanent homes for some families, according to the NT housing department.

Across the Northern Territory there are about 43 town camps, and most of them have an elected president who represents and advocates for residents.

Town camps are often in remote locations some distance from city or town centres. (ABC Alice Springs: Xavier Martin)

What is it like to live in a town camp?

Home to multi-generational families, many say they love the tight-knit nature of these communities and have adapted to the challenges they face.

Life and love inside Alice Springs’ most infamous neighbourhoods In the red centre, town camps can get a bad reputation. But the people living there say they are misunderstood, and in their homes family comes first.

As an example of the challenges, in Tennant Creek's Drive-In town camp, residents have spoken about having no electricity to run their fridges for food and medicine.

Typically, the camps' homes are not built with heating and cooling in mind, and there are calls to improve their livability and adaption to climate.

The standard of housing can also vary from camp to camp. A 2016 review commissioned by the NT government found the majority of homes in Alice Springs town camps had sheet metal roofing and were constructed in block work.

A playground in a town camp near Alice Springs. (ABC News: Mridula Amin)

While most communities had a playground, and some had basketball courts and barbecues, other issues were noticed by the 2016 review.

"Overcrowding in town camps has often been blamed for the rapid deterioration of housing conditions," the report said.

"However, it appears that it is the temporary visitors that are causing additional stress on housing."

The report found that "the most common issues [with community structures] were the shade cloths having tears, and that the general appearance was poor, based on rubbish lying around the site, graffiti, or broken equipment".

The NT government's website said it had invested $116 million in recent years in town camps, specifically in Alice Springs.

World.title: Gas vs beer: How Pocock's 57 seconds caused the government a tax headache
World.content:
It's something independent senator David Pocock has been "banging on about for years".

It was "hard to get traction", he admits.

That was, until he compared gas to beer.

A clip of him asking a government official to confirm the offshore gas tax is expected to raise less revenue than the country's tax on beer has now drawn nearly 10 million eyeballs on Instagram.

"That was the moment it just kind of reached a whole other audience," he said of the back-and-forth following a parliamentary inquiry.

Loading Instagram content

The viral moment not only captured the attention of millions, it sparked an explosion of videos demanding a 25 per cent tax on gas exports.

"Everyone knows how expensive beer is and everyone knows how much gas we export," Pocock said.

The online campaign's traction triggered a multi-million-dollar counter campaign from gas producers and left the federal government spooked.

To push back, Pocock has so far raised more than $130,000 to splash the cause on billboards across the country, including at Canberra Airport, where it will be in the face of politicians when they arrive in about a week for the federal budget.

Offers of free and discounted advertising have been rolling in too, something one of his seasoned staff members says she's never seen during 20 years of working in politics.

But with the Iran war forcing Australia to cash in on regional relationships to maintain the supply of oil, the building momentum hasn't pushed the government to act.

Gas tax campaign cuts through to community but Labor opposed The government will not increase taxes on gas giants in next month's budget, echoing the industry's argument that exporters are already paying tens of billions of dollars in taxes each year.

The prime minister this week officially killed off any options to hike taxes on the gas industry as part of the upcoming budget, warning it could threaten fuel supplies.

Speculation had been swirling for weeks, after the ABC revealed the prime minister's department had asked Treasury to model options for a windfall tax.

The hopes of gas tax proponents had been raised.

Views within cabinet were mixed, but several sources told the ABC the Pocock campaign had cut through in the community, and inside the caucus, making it politically difficult for the government to flatly rule out the tax.

Influencer and gas giants in reel contest

Alongside Senator Pocock, school teacher-turned-content creator Konrad Benjamin, better known as Punter's Politics, became a face of the campaign, with his videos consistently attracting hundreds of thousands of views.

Benjamin's content mocks the gas industry and points to research from left-wing think tank, The Australia Institute, which says a 25 per cent gas export tax would boost Commonwealth coffers by $17 billion a year.

The institute also advocates for the end of all fossil fuel exports.

Konrad Benjamin, wo goes by Punters Politics, addressed a Senate inquiry to call for a tax on gas exports. (ABC News)

Both men say they have never seen an issue generate such strong support, let alone unite voters from as politically far apart as One Nation and the Greens.

The success online of the short clips has been such that a parliamentary inquiry in April was told Shell Australia was among a handful of oil and gas companies each giving $1 million to Australian Energy Producers for an advertising blitz to counter what they've called a "misleading" tax push.

"I'm just glad that they suck at social media," Benjamin said.

"It's a heartening thing to be like, yep, you can try and buy your way in and … that's a powerful weapon that you've wielded for a long time, but we're scrappy and we're finding alternative ways to take you down," he said.

'Trillion Dollar Baby' spurred Pocock

Pocock said his interest in the topic was initially piqued after a constituent sent him a copy of the book Trillion Dollar Baby which explores Norway's gas industry.

He now reckons "we're winning the battle in terms of hearts and minds of Australians".

For Benjamin, it was that research from The Australia Institute that first got him hooked and once he started making videos about it, he says they instantly took off.

"It is very hard to gain traction on the algorithm," he said.

"But I can give you the inside hack for the algorithm at the moment: this issue," he said, noting other "influencers" had since jumped on the topic too.

Shell labels videos misleading, ramps up counter campaign

While the pair interact online, and Pocock sponsors Benjamin's lobbyist pass to parliament, they say no money is exchanged between either of them or The Australia Institute.

Regardless, their push has forced the oil and gas industry to craft a campaign highlighting the tax it does pay.

That campaign points to $22 billion in taxes and royalties paid each year — the biggest chunk of which is corporate tax, paid by any company operating in Australia.

It's a figure the prime minister has since quoted, while emphasising the importance of the gas industry.

"You do need to acknowledge the tens of billions of dollars of investment that occurs in order to have that gas extracted and without that investment that's come from North America, that's come from Japan … we wouldn't be having a debate because there wouldn't have been that extraction occur," Anthony Albanese said.

Shell Australia's Cecile Wake said the multi-million-dollar campaign was necessary to push back on the "very selective" and "misleading" arguments put forward by those in support of a new gas tax.

"It is a modest and proportionate amount to spend to put some salient facts in front of the Australian public," she told the inquiry last week.

In the last 90 days, Australian Energy Producers has spent more than $270,000 advertising with Meta, including videos featuring a man not too dissimilar to Benjamin.

The Australia Institute also spent $175,000 on Meta advertising in the same period of time, which has heavily featured its pro-gas tax stance.

Influencer says Albanese will 'pay' if no budget gas tax

Albanese points to his government's previous changes to the petroleum resource rent tax (PRRT) as evidence he has already acted.

"The PRRT reforms are designed so that there will be increased taxes paid over a period of time," he said on Wednesday.

While any proposal for further taxes is on ice for now, the government's pre-budget modelling of options does leave the door open for future consideration of changes.

But according to Benjamin, the time is now.

As an influential creator with 570,000 followers on Instagram, he's warning he'll set about to politically punish Albanese (who has 640,000 followers) if he doesn't initiate a new gas tax in the budget.

"If he doesn't listen, then he must pay the price and that is an electoral defeat," he said.

"I will do everything in my power to make Albanese pay.

"I will do everything I can to make sure that everybody knows who is to blame for this not being fixed, and that's democracy, because if this politician won't do what we want, we have to find another one who will."

World.title: Donald Trump's 'wishful thinking' over his blockade of Iranian oil
World.content:
As the United States has tightened its grip on Iranian ports through its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, Tehran has been forced to stockpile oil that would have otherwise been exported.

But while some commentators believe that Iran will run out of space to store it in less than a fortnight, regime watchers warn Tehran has been preparing for this moment.

Iran has been stashing its primary export commodity in storage tanks and ships off the coast in an effort to avoid reducing the amount it is pumping out of its rich oil fields.

Iran war live updates: For the latest news on the Middle East crisis, read our blog.

Turning off the taps, or reducing output much further, could put the regime's infrastructure at risk, according to some analysts and US President Donald Trump's administration.

But Iran's domestic consumption means supply will always be needed. And thanks to the oil the regime had stockpiled outside the war zone before the conflict began, there is plenty of supply to trade beyond the blockade.

This sets up a "game of chicken", according to senior analyst and Iran program director at the International Crisis Group, Ali Vaez.

"The Iranians believe that they have more staying power than the other side and, of course, the United States has the exact opposite belief," he said.

"This is why the diplomatic track is stalemated."

Independent analysis of how much oil Iran is producing and storing while its tankers are unable to sail, shows pressure is building — both in terms of how much the regime can really stockpile and the pain its already-ravaged economy can endure.

But while diplomacy falters and both sides contemplate a return to strikes, Iran is looking at overland options to bypass the blockade, move its oil and reconnect its economic lifeline.

The blockade is working

The US blockade came into effect at midday on April 13. Since then, just a small number of Iranian ships have made it past the American warships patrolling the waters west of the Strait of Hormuz.

Those ships, though, were cargo ships and not carrying oil.

"No confirmed tanker has exited the US blockade zone," head of crude oil analysis at commodity data company Kpler, Homayoun Falakshahi, said.

If ships are being fired upon and seized how can there be a ceasefire? As part of its blockade of Iran, ships have been seized by US forces, others fired upon by Iran and, most recently, boarded by the regime's revolutionary guards. This is all while both sides maintain there is a ceasefire.

He said several Iranian tankers did cross the Strait of Hormuz but failed to clear the blockade and "most vessels instead diverted toward the Chabahar area in southern Iran."

Michelle Bockmann is a senior maritime intelligence analyst with Windward, a maritime analysis firm, and has been looking closely at the marine data in the region since the blockade came into place.

"Looking at what has got through, or more importantly what hasn't, it is clear the US blockade has curtailed most, if not all, crude oil shipment from Iran," she said.

When the war broke out in late February, and Iran took control of the Strait of Hormuz, the regime's revolutionary guards effectively closed the vital shipping waterway to much of the world's tanker traffic.

Iran cut off importing nations, including Australia, from other suppliers in the Persian Gulf and trapped much of the region's oil on the eastern side of the strait.

But Iran's fleet continued to sail and, before the US blockade kicked in, the regime was exporting even more than before the war.

"In February, Iran sort of knew this was coming and they whacked all the oil they could on tankers to get them out," Ms Bockmann said.

"In March, Iran had its blockade but [it was] business as usual for those tankers.

"Then after April 13, [there was] an immediate reduction … and now two weeks later, no Iranian vessels laden with oil have arrived in Asia," she said.

Mr Falakshahi had a similar analysis, saying: "Iran's exports remained resilient pre-blockade, averaging 1.85 million barrels per day [mbd] in March, above the 1.7 mbd prior trend [seen in the previous three months]."

But export loadings "dropped sharply to 567,000 barrels per day post-blockade."

"The regime did anticipate the possibility of a US naval blockade because they had watched what the US did in Venezuela in the run-up to the war with Iran," Mr Vaez said.

"They had put in place contingency plans … they had pre-sold some of their oil to China, shipping it to places like Malaysia. They actually did develop a cushion."

But with much less oil leaving Iranian territory, two other metrics come into play: how much oil Iran is producing and how much it can store.

Mr Falakshahi's analysis estimates that the production cuts already underway inside Iran's oil industry could see a further reduction of 1.5 mbd by mid-May.

"If the blockade is lifted by late May, production should recover quickly," Mr Falakshahi said.

But if it doesn't, Iran could run out of storage and be forced to further taper off production.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently posted on X, saying Iran's primary export terminal on Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf was "soon nearing capacity".

The island 24 kilometres off the coast of Iran is central to the nation's economic lifeline, with 90 per cent of Iran's crude oil coming through its terminal.

Mr Bessent said Kharg at capacity would force the regime to reduce production further and estimated the cost would be "an additional approximately $US170 million [$236 million] per day in lost revenue" and cause "permanent damage to Iran's oil infrastructure."

Mr Vaez cautioned against completely accepting the US narrative.

"This concept that President Trump has talked about of Iranian storage capacity exploding soon, I think is wishful thinking," he said.

"Undoubtedly, the blockade is hurting the Iranians, but one has to also remember that this is a very resilient economy that has been living under sanctions for many years,"

"It has a very high threshold of pain and no hesitation to basically transfer that pain to a population."

Kpler analysis did estimate regime revenues would eventually be hit by up to $US250 million a day, but noted that would take some time to really be felt by Iran, possibly "three to four months from now".

As Iranian oil continues to flow through its network of pipelines with fewer places to really go, some analysts have forecasted how much storage capacity Iran has left, both in terms of physical space as well as the number of days until it is full.

Kpler analysis from earlier this week estimated Iran had the equivalent of about 12 days of normal export volumes left for crude oil at its onshore storage facilities.

But with no oil making it through the blockade, there are ships across the region that become floating storage facilities too.

Iran's storage solutions

Its inability to ship the oil has forced Iran to get creative about where it can park it until a deal is done to see it sail past the US warships off its coastline.

"There are so many vessels trapped, west of Hormuz … these vessels haven't gone anywhere," Ms Bockmann said.

And every barrel that cannot be shipped needs to be stored.

Data analysed by Windward and seen by the ABC shows ghost ships and ships using "spoofing techniques" inside the Persian Gulf.

It is likely Iran is using these ships to store oil to delay slowing or stopping production.

"They are using everything they can get their hands on at the moment because nobody wants to shut in production," Ms Bockmann said.

There has been some speculation that if Iran was forced to shut down its oil production, its aging machinery would be at risk of not restarting again or not reaching pre-existing levels of production.

Analysis of Iran's storage capacity looks at onshore facilities as well as nearby ships in the Gulf that become floating stockpiles.

Kpler analysis now estimates there are 18 tankers in the Persian Gulf, Gulf of Oman and near Pakistan that have a history of lifting Iranian crude oil that could become part of its storage fleet.

Some of the ships identified by Kpler have gone long stretches of time without turning tracking transponders on, signalling they are likely either part of shadow fleets moving across global shipping lanes or aging ships that are now being called up to be used as storage.

For example, the Iranian-flagged Navarz is a crude oil tanker now believed to be trapped in the Persian Gulf. But this vessel's voyage history is patchy, and according to Kpler marine tracking data, it has not reported a position in several years. Kpler now believes it is at least partly available to the regime for storage.

The 1996-built Nasha is speculated to be a ghost ship being used to store oil by Iran. (Marine Traffic: Rik van Marle)

Similarly, the aging vessel the Nasha has no evidence of use within the past 12 months, but analysis of satellite imagery now places it off Kharg Island.

Storage for oil that would have otherwise been shipped is finite, but according to Mr Vaez, domestic consumption means the wells won't run dry.

He said Iran only exported about half of the oil it produced and even if the regime reduced its oil production, it "can still keep all of their wells open and use that material domestically".

The risks of storing oil on ships

Iran holds 184 million barrels of oil "on water" currently, according to Kpler analysis.

Of that, 60 million barrels are effectively stuck in the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman behind the US blockade.

Jennifer Parker is a former naval officer with experience in the Middle East.

She said it was possible Iran was using old ships to store oil, but "it isn't without challenges".

"It depends on how many of these ships they have available, and how safe they are in terms of not leaking," she said.

Ships identified by analysts as likely being used to store Iranian oil were built up to 30 years ago.

In 2023, the UN had to extract an oil tanker off the coast of Yemen that had been storing more than 1 billion barrels of oil for eight years.

The operation to avoid an explosive catastrophe in the Red Sea For eight years, a rusted tanker carrying more than 1 million barrels of oil has sat neglected in the Red Sea, threatening to cause the world's worst oil-spill disaster. After years of planning, a daring salvage operation is now underway.

It was a delicate and risky operation and the first of its kind to be done, but the alternative posed a greater challenge.

If the aging, decaying ship in the Red Sea had spilled the oil, the natural disaster would have had the potential to wipe out one of the world's largest marine ecosystems.

This storage tactic could also become a target.

"If the US recommence the hot end of the conflict, they may well target these vessels," Ms Parker said.

She said the US–Israel attack on Iran was two-phased. The first phase was the military action, the attacks on some infrastructure.

"That was about degrading the military and, of course, degrading the political elite," she added.

The second and current phase is about cranking up the economic pressure.

"If you can shut off a country from being able to get its goods in and out by the sea, then you can economically coerce them," Ms Parker said.

Ms Bockman agreed, saying: "Each day the blockade is in place, the more desperate Iran will be to end this impasse and prevent the shut-in of oil production."

Both sides under pressure

US President Donald Trump has taken pride in his "genius" idea of the blockade.

"The blockade has been 100 per cent foolproof," he told reporters on Thursday in the Oval Office.

Mr Trump said if Iran wanted to end the blockade and save their "dead economy", all they had to do was "say, 'we give up, we give up'".

Donald Trump has said the blockade is "100 per cent foolproof" but Iran is working on contingencies. (Reuters: Marco Bello)

But again, as a close watcher of the regime, Mr Vaez that warned those now making decisions in Tehran were again coming up with contingencies.

"This is a big country that has 15 neighbours through land and sea," he said.

"They have also alternative routes, pathways through land, through Pakistan, railroads through Afghanistan and Iraq, Türkiye, the Caucasus, the Caspian Sea."

Pakistan has been playing the role of peace broker in this war, but it has also made changes internally and announced a new trade corridor with Iran.

As the war enters its third month, the US is attempting to really ratchet up pressure on Iran's economy and is being very vocal about that.

Analysts believe the "economic coercion" from all sides is designed to bring Iran back to the negotiating table.

Ms Parker said any loss of revenues impacted the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps's "ability to fight, their ability to rebuild, but also the morale" within militant group.

While in the US, Mr Trump is under some pressure over the rising price of fuel and the cost of the war to the public purse.

Most analysts agree that the war will likely end via negotiations, but when that happens depends on how much pressure either side is under.

Mr Vaez said the generals making regime decisions, while feeling the economic strain, likely believed they could withstand the blockade for "another two to three months".

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Alleged killer of five-year-old NT girl moved to Darwin after riots in Alice Springs; Trump tells US Congress operations in Iran have ‘terminated’
World.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is leading calls for calm in Alice Springs as a massive police presence heads to the town to help maintain a fragile peace after the arrest of an accused child killer led to vigilantism and street riots.

There are now multiple calls for inquiries and the central Australian town has brought in an alcohol ban as part of the efforts to prevent further outbreaks of violence after Jefferson Lewis handed himself into a town camp near Charles Creek. He was beaten unconscious by community members.

Loading

Lewis, 47, was arrested by police on Thursday night after one of the Northern Territory’s biggest manhunts following the disappearance of five-year-old girl, Kumanjayi Little Baby, who was abducted from her bed at Old Timers Aboriginal Camp on Saturday and found dead by a river bed five days later. The cause of death is yet to be determined.

The national commissioner for Indigenous children called for an investigation into the correctional systems that allowed the recent release of Lewis.

World.title: How Maguire defied his critics to become ‘one of the best signings’ in Broncos’ history
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

All it took was Payne Haas announcing his departure from the Brisbane Broncos for the claws to come out, and critics to condemn Michael Maguire as a man fighting for his coaching future. Four months earlier, he had broken a 19-year premiership drought. A ball had not yet been kicked in 2026. “The bigger the club the more scrutiny. You can either use it as a motivator or let it get to you,” Broncos legend Darren Lockyer told this masthead. “I choose the former. I think Madge would’ve channelled that criticism ... and used it as motivation to the playing group to prove a point.” Michael Maguire was under pressure from the start of his tenure at the Broncos. Zak Simmonds Poor defeats to Hull KR, Penrith and Parramatta were followed by Ben Te’o’s exit as assistant coach, the eruption of a war of words with Gordon Tallis, and an injury toll reaching 13 squad members. Haas’ defection to South Sydney sparked speculation Maguire had lost his locker room, and his hard-line methods were wearing thin.



Yet the past two weeks – two triumphs, with more than $5 million worth of talent sidelined – have silenced the doubters. “I put him right up there as one of the best signings we’ve ever made,” Broncos chief executive Dave Donaghy said. “He’s got a way about him I have deep admiration and respect for. The way he moves in an organisation and connects his group, they’re really special attributes he has.” Loading Pressure and expectation were always going to follow Maguire. He succeeded a club great in Kevin Walters, and had developed a reputation as a hard taskmaster at South Sydney and Wests Tigers. Brisbane’s six titles had all been led by Wayne Bennett, with Ivan Henjak, Anthony Griffin, Anthony Seibold, Walters and even Bennett shown the door from 2010. It speaks to the demands of leading a club boasting close to 70,000 members.



“I think everyone understands when they come into the organisation there’s a real responsibility to add to the legacy. We understand the interest around our club, and I’d much rather be relevant than not,” Donaghy said. Related Article NRL 2026 PNG has the world’s second-worst crime rate. But a ‘suit of armour’ eases the NRL’s fears “The club’s based in the heart of Brisbane, we play at Suncorp Stadium and there’s a 45,000 average crowd – effectively akin to having a State of Origin every second week. “There’s always expectation. I’m sure this has been a different experience for him, but he’s been outstanding for our club.” A long tenure could beckon, once the time comes to assess a contract extension beyond the end of Maguire’s 2027 deal. “Madge and I have known each other long enough to have that discussion when the time is right, and we’ll know when the time is right,” Donaghy said. “He’s really clear around where he wants to take the group, he’s really clear around where he sees the group’s potential. We’ll make sure myself and others play that role to help him achieve sustainable success.”



While Lockyer is “wary” about giving too many “pats on the back”, several Broncos have become bona fide stars under Maguire’s tutelage. Xavier Willison has announced himself as the Broncos’ long-term forward pack leader, producing the sort of statistics often reserved for the injured Haas. This was the same enforcer who could be seen throwing up in back field throughout the preseason. Now, he has shown a path beyond Haas, with Lockyer confident he could “take on Payne’s influence over the team when he leaves”.



Gehamat Shibasaki, Ben Talty and Josiah Karapani are others who have become mainstays after receiving lifelines by Maguire. “That doesn’t happen by accident,” Donaghy said, “that happens by a design and a deliberate intent.” That success has come down to enhanced fitness levels, and Reece Walsh has perhaps become the most prominent example. Walsh – who returns from a fractured cheekbone in Saturday’s clash against the Roosters – became the NRL’s poster boy on the back of his attacking wizardry. But under Maguire, the fullback has shown a willingness to do the tough stuff. “Without a doubt the work they’ve put in to get physically fit has helped him mentally,” Lockyer said.

World.title: Here’s what should be in the sequel to the Michael Jackson biopic
World.content:
Analysis CultureMoviesMichael Jackson Here’s what should be in the sequel to the Michael Jackson biopic George Palathingal May 2, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Michael, Antoine Fuqua’s dazzling but slight film on the life of the divisive self-proclaimed King of Pop Michael Jackson, has dominated the worldwide box office over the past week or so. And, given how much money it has made, and how much more it is going to make, the inevitable sequel has been announced. It’s easy to see why the film has been a success. It’s extraordinarily entertaining, featuring an electrifying turn by the pop titan’s nephew, Jaafar Jackson, in the title role. The re-creations of several iconic performances (the Don’t Stop ’til You Get Enough, Beat It and Thriller videos, the Victory and Bad tours and, perhaps best of all, Billie Jean at Motown 25) might be clumsily strung together by some token narrative about Michael wanting to break free from bad dad Joe, but they are undeniably spectacular. The film has also provoked debate over the omission of any mention of the child abuse allegations against Michael Jackson, most notably in 1993, 2003 and even after his death (in 2009) with the 2019 documentary Leaving Neverland. An early draft of the Michael script apparently did address at least the 1993 case but the biopic had to be reworked when a clause was discovered from the legal settlement with then-13-year-old accuser Jordan Chandler, which prohibited the film’s makers from any dramatisation of Chandler’s story. As for a sequel? They should make two.



Related Article Box office Bad reviews, off the wall numbers for Michael Jackson biopic The fear some seem to have is the filmmakers have used all the best bits with the first film, but these doubters are sorely mistaken. A first sequel can pick up where Michael left off with, if not Martin Scorsese’s Bad video that starred Wesley Snipes, the sensational ’30s gangster pastiche of Smooth Criminal, also from the Bad album and directed by the less heralded Colin Chilvers. Jaafar has already said he wants a crack at that and, now he has proved himself as a superstar in his own right, he’d absolutely be back to do it. Paul McCartney probably won’t authorise his likeness for his fantastic duets with Michael Jackson (The Girl Is Mine and Say Say Say) after Jackson bought the Beatles catalogue from under his nose, and sister Janet wanted no part of Michael (making the ignoring of her very existence in the movie feel suitably odd), so we’re not going to see their Scream collab. But Stevie Wonder sang at Jackson’s funeral, so he might still love him enough to let someone play him for the recording of Just Good Friends. There are also re-creations waiting to happen of the glorious, ironically colourful Black or White video, a delve into Jackson’s unlikely marriage to Lisa Marie Presley and their You Are Not Alone film clip, and even the pompous, overblown but enormously popular Earth Song. (Again, it’s highly unlikely that they’d portray Jarvis Cocker from Pulp’s heroic stage invasion of Jackson’s distasteful, Christ-wannabe performance at the 1996 Brit awards, but we live in hope.)



And if they do run out of videos to remake, there are always live performances of classics they missed the first time that they can have a crack at. Jackson always liked to dramatically break down in tears on stage during She’s Out of My Life, for example, and there was no room in the first film for, say, PYT or the frankly awesome Man in the Mirror. What will the narrative be, second time around? Well, it barely mattered for the first movie, so I wouldn’t lose too much sleep over that. Vaguely stringing together the above musical beats has “hit sequel” written all over it regardless. A second sequel, however, would be less crowd-pleasing but more interesting. Here we could get the film the detractors wanted. This wouldn’t be authorised, so the makers wouldn’t get the tunes, but that wouldn’t matter – the fans would have the first two movies for those, and Jackson’s last proper album, 2001’s Invincible, was rubbish anyway. And so this film’s makers could dive deep into the stuff no one in the family wants to talk about: the child abuse allegations. Jaafar, being part of the family, probably wouldn’t come back for this one – but again, that wouldn’t matter because his uncle looked so different by then you could comfortably recast the role. The second sequel could thus have a radically lower budget and take a grittier, indie-style approach.



After the success of Bohemian Rhapsody – like Michael, also from producer Graham King – that film’s makers missed a trick not getting Rami Malek back to star in a lower-key, serious, “prestige” sequel on Freddie Mercury’s real final years, leading up to his death. A final, unauthorised film on Michael Jackson could complete an unprecedented trilogy in comparable – and satisfying – fashion. George Palathingal is a senior music writer.
